conflicts.name: The Rwandan genocide and the churches
conflicts.religionRoleNote: The genocide of the Tutsi was not a religious war: killers and victims overwhelmingly shared the same Catholic and Protestant churches, and the organisers' ideology was ethnic and political ('Hutu Power'). Religion's role lies in the churches' long entanglement with the state and with racialised ethnic categories. Historians such as Ian Linden and Timothy Longman show how missionaries and bishops first championed a Tutsi elite under Belgian rule, then from the 1950s backed the 'Hutu revolution', and how senior clergy stayed closely tied to President Habyarimana's single-party regime. Longman argues that church hierarchies taught obedience to authority and tolerated ethnic discrimination, so that many parishioners saw no contradiction between churchgoing and killing; others, including Rwandan Catholic writers, stress that the hierarchy did not plan the genocide, that many clergy were themselves murdered, and that individual Christians of all churches risked their lives to shelter Tutsi. The debate is over the degree of institutional responsibility, not over the fact that churches became killing grounds and that some clergy took part.

sides.name: Interim government, Rwandan Armed Forces (FAR) and the Interahamwe and Impuzamugambi militias ('Hutu Power')
sides.faith: Overwhelmingly baptised Catholics and Protestants; the ideology was ethnic nationalism, not religion

sides.name: Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) and its army
sides.faith: Mainly Tutsi exiles of Christian background; a secular political-military movement

sides.name: Victims: Tutsi civilians and Hutu political opponents and moderates
sides.faith: Catholic, Protestant, Adventist and Muslim Rwandans

conflicts.summary: Between April and July 1994 Hutu extremists organised the murder of roughly half a million to 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, in about a hundred days. Rwanda was one of the most Christianised countries in Africa, and many of the worst massacres happened inside churches where Tutsi had sought sanctuary; some priests, pastors and nuns helped the killers, while others died protecting the hunted. The genocide forced the Catholic, Anglican, Adventist and other churches into a painful reckoning with their political alliances and their teaching about ethnicity.
conflicts.story:
Rwanda's Catholic mission was founded by the White Fathers in 1900, and under Belgian rule after the First World War the church worked hand in hand with the colonial state. Belgian administrators and missionaries such as Bishop Léon Classe treated the Tutsi minority as a natural ruling caste and favoured them in schools and chiefships; ethnic identity cards were introduced in 1933–34. After King Mutara III Rudahigwa's baptism and the dedication of Rwanda to Christ the King in 1946, mass conversion made the country overwhelmingly Christian. In the 1950s a new generation of missionaries, sympathetic to Christian democracy and the Hutu majority, changed sides: the Hutu Manifesto of 1957 was co-written by Grégoire Kayibanda, a former seminarian and editor of the Catholic paper Kinyamateka, and Archbishop André Perraudin's 1959 Lenten letter was read by many as endorsing the Hutu cause. The 'social revolution' of 1959–62 drove tens of thousands of Tutsi into exile, and periodic massacres followed.

Under President Juvénal Habyarimana (1973–94) the churches remained close to the ruling party, the MRND. Archbishop Vincent Nsengiyumva of Kigali sat on its central committee until Vatican pressure obliged him to step down around 1990, and Anglican and some Protestant leaders were similarly tied to the regime. When the Rwandan Patriotic Front, formed by Tutsi refugees in Uganda, invaded in October 1990, the government answered with propaganda against Tutsi as 'inyenzi' (cockroaches), local massacres and the arming of party militias. Some Christian voices, including the journalist-priest André Sibomana and a number of Catholic and Protestant clergy, publicly denounced these abuses; church leaders also helped broker the Arusha Accords of August 1993, which promised power-sharing.

On the evening of 6 April 1994 Habyarimana's aircraft was shot down over Kigali. Within hours the Presidential Guard and militias began killing opposition politicians, including Prime Minister Agathe Uwilingiyimana, and Tutsi civilians, using lists prepared in advance. Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines urged listeners to 'work' and leave no Tutsi alive. Local officials, soldiers and the Interahamwe gathered people at roadblocks, communal offices, schools and churches, then killed them with firearms, grenades, machetes and clubs. Sexual violence against Tutsi women was systematic. UN peacekeepers (UNAMIR) were cut to a token force after ten Belgian soldiers were murdered, and outside powers declined to intervene.

Churches, traditional places of refuge in earlier pogroms, became sites of mass murder. At Ntarama and Nyamata in Bugesera thousands were killed inside and around the church buildings in mid-April; at Nyange the parish priest Athanase Seromba was convicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) of helping to organise the bulldozing of his church on some 2,000 refugees. The Adventist pastor Elizaphan Ntakirutimana was convicted by the ICTR for his part in the attacks on Mugonero mission, and two Benedictine nuns of Sovu were convicted by a Belgian court in 2001 for complicity in killings at their convent. At the same time Christians of every denomination, and Rwandan Muslims, hid neighbours; among those killed for doing so was Sister Félicité Niyitegeka, who refused to abandon the people she was sheltering at Gisenyi. More than 200 priests, religious and pastors were killed, Tutsi and Hutu alike.

The RPF, led by Paul Kagame, renewed its offensive in April and advanced through the east and centre. Its soldiers also committed reprisal killings of civilians: a 1994 UNHCR mission led by Robert Gersony estimated that tens of thousands died at their hands, and on 5 June 1994 RPF soldiers at Gakurazo near Kabgayi killed Archbishop Nsengiyumva, Bishops Thaddée Nsengiyumva and Joseph Ruzindana and about ten priests. French troops entered the south-west in June under Operation Turquoise. Kigali fell to the RPF on 4 July, and by mid-July the interim government, army and some two million Hutu civilians had fled, largely into Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo), where the refugee camps became bases for the defeated forces and the region's later wars.

The UN Security Council established the ICTR at Arusha in November 1994; it convicted the former prime minister Jean Kambanda, Bagosora and others, as well as clergy. Inside Rwanda, mass trials were handled from 2002 by community gacaca courts. Several church buildings, including Ntarama and Nyamata, were turned into national memorials where the victims' bones and clothing are displayed. The relationship between the new government and the churches, especially the Catholic Church, remained tense for years over accusations of complicity and clergy who escaped to Europe.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Genocidal propaganda was ethnic rather than theological, but it borrowed religious idiom: extremist media cast the Tutsi as foreign invaders, and some Hutu Power publications and speakers presented the extermination as a duty and even claimed divine favour. Historic Catholic teaching had long been used to legitimise first Tutsi and then Hutu rule, and the hierarchy's public statements in April 1994 called for peace in general terms without naming the genocide or the government. Killers often attended Mass, and some reportedly paused to pray before resuming the slaughter, which survivors and later Rwandan church leaders described as the deepest betrayal of the gospel.
religiousCauses: Missionary and colonial 'Hamitic' theory, taught in mission schools, portrayed Tutsi as alien Nilotic conquerors and Hutu as native Bantu, hardening ethnic categories that propaganda later exploited.
The Catholic Church first sponsored a Tutsi elite and then, from the 1950s, the Hutu counter-elite, so that ethnic politics and church politics became intertwined.
Senior clergy's membership of or closeness to the ruling MRND party compromised the churches' ability to criticise government violence before and during 1994.
A culture of deference to authority, reinforced in church teaching and practice, made it harder for congregations to resist orders from local officials, as Timothy Longman argues.
Previous massacres (1959–63, 1973, 1990–93) had gone unpunished and were seldom forcefully condemned by church hierarchies, which encouraged impunity.
otherCauses: Colonial racialisation of Hutu and Tutsi identities, including the ethnic identity cards introduced by the Belgian administration in 1933–34.
The civil war that began with the RPF invasion of October 1990 and Hutu extremists' fear of losing power under the Arusha Accords.
Economic crisis after the collapse of coffee prices in the late 1980s, land scarcity and structural adjustment.
A centralised, highly organised state with administrative structures down to the hill level that could mobilise the population.
Hate media such as Kangura and Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines, and the arming of party militias.
International passivity, including the reduction of UNAMIR in April 1994 and the reluctance of the UN Security Council to use the word 'genocide'.
triggers: The shooting down of President Habyarimana's aircraft over Kigali on 6 April 1994, which also killed Burundi's president Cyprien Ntaryamira.
The immediate murder of moderate politicians, including Prime Minister Agathe Uwilingiyimana, by the Presidential Guard on 7 April.
The withdrawal of most UN peacekeepers after the killing of ten Belgian soldiers, which signalled to the organisers that there would be no intervention.

timeline.text: The White Fathers found the first Catholic mission in Rwanda at Save.
Belgian authorities issue identity cards recording each Rwandan's ethnicity as Hutu, Tutsi or Twa.
The Hutu Manifesto, co-written by Grégoire Kayibanda, a Catholic journalist close to the mission, demands an end to Tutsi dominance.
Archbishop André Perraudin's Lenten pastoral letter on charity and justice; the 'Hutu revolution' begins and Tutsi flee into exile.
The RPF invades from Uganda on 1 October; the government responds with mass arrests and local massacres of Tutsi.
The Arusha Accords, supported by church mediators, provide for power-sharing; the UNAMIR peacekeeping force is deployed.
6 April: Habyarimana's plane is shot down and the genocide begins; in mid-April thousands are killed in the churches of Ntarama and Nyamata.
5 June: RPF soldiers kill three Catholic bishops and about ten priests at Gakurazo near Kabgayi.
4 July: Kigali falls to the RPF; in November the UN creates the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.
A Belgian court convicts two Benedictine nuns of Sovu for complicity in genocide.
The ICTR convicts Fr Athanase Seromba over the destruction of Nyange church; his sentence is raised to life imprisonment on appeal in 2008.
Rwanda's Catholic bishops issue a formal apology for the part played by members of the church in the genocide.
Pope Francis, meeting President Kagame in the Vatican, asks forgiveness for the 'sins and failings of the Church and its members'.

keyPeople.name: André Perraudin
keyPeople.focus: His 1959 pastoral letter, which condemned social injustice against the Hutu majority, was read as church support for the Hutu revolution.
keyPeople.outcome: Remained a respected figure to the post-independence regime and a symbol to critics of the church's ethnic politics.

keyPeople.name: Vincent Nsengiyumva
keyPeople.focus: A close ally of President Habyarimana who sat on the ruling party's central committee; criticised for failing to denounce the genocide clearly.
keyPeople.outcome: Killed by RPF soldiers at Gakurazo on 5 June 1994 with two other bishops and several priests.

keyPeople.name: Athanase Seromba
keyPeople.focus: Convicted of helping to organise the demolition of his church on Tutsi refugees in April 1994.
keyPeople.outcome: Fled to Italy and worked as a priest under another name; surrendered to the ICTR in 2002 and was sentenced on appeal to life imprisonment.

keyPeople.name: Elizaphan Ntakirutimana
keyPeople.focus: Convicted by the ICTR of aiding and abetting the attack on Tutsi who had taken refuge at the Mugonero Adventist complex, in a case that also convicted his son.
keyPeople.outcome: Extradited from the United States, sentenced in 2003 to ten years and released shortly before his death.

keyPeople.name: Félicité Niyitegeka
keyPeople.role: Hutu religious sister of the Auxiliaires de l'Apostolat
keyPeople.focus: Sheltered Tutsi at Gisenyi and helped them escape to Zaire; refused her brother's offer of safety unless those with her were spared.
keyPeople.outcome: Killed by militiamen on 21 April 1994; honoured by the Rwandan state as a national hero.

keyPeople.name: André Sibomana
keyPeople.role: Catholic priest and editor of Kinyamateka
keyPeople.focus: Exposed human rights abuses and corruption before 1994, hid people during the genocide and afterwards also criticised abuses by the new government.
keyPeople.outcome: Died in 1998; his interviews were published as Hope for Rwanda.

keyPeople.name: Paul Kagame
keyPeople.role: Commander of the Rwandan Patriotic Army
keyPeople.focus: Led the RPF offensive that ended the genocide; his forces were also responsible for reprisal killings of civilians and clergy.
keyPeople.outcome: Vice-president from 1994 and president of Rwanda from 2000.

casualties.note: Range for victims of the genocide, overwhelmingly Tutsi. Alison Des Forges (Human Rights Watch, 1999) estimated at least half a million; demographic studies (e.g. Marijke Verpoorten) suggest around 600,000 Tutsi, roughly three-quarters of the Tutsi population; the Rwandan government's 2002 census of victims counted over one million, including Hutu victims. Not included: Hutu killed by the RPF in 1994, which a UNHCR team led by Robert Gersony estimated at roughly 25,000–45,000 between April and August, and the far larger death toll of the subsequent wars in Zaire/Congo.

effects: The RPF took power, ending the genocide and establishing the government that has ruled Rwanda since 1994.
Some two million refugees fled to Zaire, Tanzania and Burundi; armed camps in eastern Zaire helped trigger the Congo wars of 1996–2003.
The ICTR (1994–2015) produced the first international convictions for genocide and recognised rape as an act of genocide (Akayesu, 1998).
Rwanda's gacaca courts tried well over a million cases between 2002 and 2012.
Ethnic identity cards were abolished and public use of Hutu and Tutsi categories was strongly discouraged by law.
effectsOnChurch: Churches such as Ntarama, Nyamata and Nyange were left as genocide memorials; many congregations no longer had a building or a pastor.
Hundreds of clergy and religious were killed, and others were tried or fled, leaving church structures devastated.

The Catholic Church's credibility in Rwanda was badly damaged; the government accused it of complicity and of protecting suspects abroad, while the Vatican initially stressed individual rather than institutional guilt.
Rwandan Catholic bishops apologised in 2016 and Pope Francis asked forgiveness in 2017; Protestant churches also issued confessions, notably the Detmold confession of 1996.
Many Rwandans left the historic churches for Pentecostal congregations, and Islam gained respect for the record of Muslim rescuers.
conflicts.legacy: The Rwandan genocide is the starkest modern case of mass atrocity inside a predominantly Christian society, and it is studied in seminaries and churches as a warning about church–state alliances, ethnic loyalty and the failure of preaching to shape conduct. It is also remembered for the rescuers, clergy and lay, who died rather than hand over their neighbours.

dissenters.name: Félicité Niyitegeka
dissenters.text: A Hutu sister who chose to die with the Tutsi she had been sheltering rather than accept safety for herself alone.

dissenters.name: André Sibomana
dissenters.text: Priest-journalist who denounced the regime's abuses from 1990, hid potential victims in 1994 and afterwards insisted that all crimes, including the RPF's, be acknowledged.

dissenters.name: Rwandan Muslims of Biryogo and elsewhere
dissenters.text: Muslim communities widely sheltered Tutsi and refused to join the killing, an example frequently cited by Rwandan Christians in later self-examination.

dissenters.name: Pope John Paul II
dissenters.text: In May 1994 he publicly described the killings as a genocide, before many governments would use the word, and called on Catholics not to take part.

dissenters.name: Pope Francis
dissenters.text: In 2017 asked forgiveness for the sins and failings of the church and its members, 'among whom priests, and religious men and women' who succumbed to hatred and violence.

campaigns.title: The RPF offensive of April–July 1994
campaigns.people: Rwandan Patriotic Army under Paul Kagame
campaigns.text: From its northern base the RPF pushed south and east, taking Byumba in April, Kabgayi in early June (where the bishops were killed), Gitarama in mid-June and Kigali on 4 July, then swept west to Ruhengeri and Gisenyi, driving the interim government and its army into Zaire by mid-July.

campaigns.title: The flight of the interim government and Hutu civilians
campaigns.people: Interim government, FAR, militias and some two million civilians
campaigns.text: The interim government moved from Kigali to Gitarama and then Gisenyi before crossing into Zaire in July, accompanied by a mass exodus of civilians; cholera killed tens of thousands in the Goma camps, which the former army and militias soon controlled.

conflicts.name: Joseph Kony and the Lord's Resistance Army
conflicts.region: Northern Uganda, South Sudan, north-eastern DR Congo and the Central African Republic
conflicts.religionRoleNote: The LRA grew out of Alice Auma 'Lakwena's' Holy Spirit Movement and kept a spirit-possession cosmology mixing Catholic and Protestant elements, Acholi spirit beliefs and later some Islamic practices: Joseph Kony claimed to be guided by spirits, invoked the Ten Commandments and imposed ritual rules. Anthropologists such as Heike Behrend and Kristof Titeca argue that this spiritual order was real to commanders and abductees and essential to discipline. Most specialists (Tim Allen, Sverker Finnström, Adam Branch) nevertheless locate the war's causes in the north–south divide in Ugandan politics, the Acholi's loss of power after 1986, the National Resistance Army's abuses and Sudanese state backing. The movement had no coherent Christian programme, its violence fell overwhelmingly on Acholi Christians, and churches led the search for peace, so religion was a contributing and legitimising factor rather than the cause.

sides.name: Lord's Resistance Army (earlier the Holy Spirit Movement and allied rebel groups)
sides.faith: Syncretic spirit cult using Christian, Acholi and some Islamic elements

sides.name: Government of Uganda: National Resistance Army, later Uganda People's Defence Force (UPDF), and local militias
sides.faith: Secular state; most soldiers and leaders Christian

sides.name: Government of Sudan (supporter of the LRA c. 1994–2005)
sides.faith: Islamist government in Khartoum

sides.name: Acholi and neighbouring civilians
sides.faith: Predominantly Catholic and Anglican Christians, with Muslims and traditional believers

conflicts.summary: For more than two decades the Lord's Resistance Army waged a war of abduction, mutilation and massacre in northern Uganda and later across three neighbouring countries. Its leader Joseph Kony claimed spiritual guidance and spoke of ruling by the Ten Commandments, yet most of its victims were Acholi Christians, including tens of thousands of abducted children forced to fight and serve. The government's counter-insurgency, especially forced encampment of almost the whole Acholi population, caused further mass suffering. Catholic, Anglican and Muslim leaders in Acholiland became the most prominent advocates of amnesty and negotiation.
conflicts.story:
When Yoweri Museveni's National Resistance Army (NRA) seized power in January 1986, it defeated a national army dominated by northerners, many of them Acholi. Former soldiers fled north, and NRA abuses in Acholiland, including killings, looting of cattle and detentions, fed resistance. Several armed groups emerged, among them the Uganda People's Democratic Army. The most remarkable was the Holy Spirit Movement of Alice Auma, a spirit medium who said she was possessed by the spirit Lakwena. Her 'Holy Spirit Mobile Forces' were bound by twenty 'Holy Spirit Safety Precautions', anointed with shea-nut oil said to turn bullets to water, and promised to purify Uganda. In 1987 they marched south and were defeated near Jinja late that year; Alice fled to Kenya, where she died in a refugee camp in 2007.

Joseph Kony, a young man from Odek near Gulu who had served as an altar boy and was reputedly related to Alice, had begun his own spirit-led group in 1987. Absorbing remnants of other rebel forces, it became known by the early 1990s as the Lord's Resistance Army. After Betty Bigombe's peace talks collapsed in early 1994, Sudan's government, at war with southern rebels supported by Uganda, gave the LRA bases, arms and supplies. With few adult recruits, the LRA relied on abduction: boys were made fighters and porters, girls were given to commanders as 'wives', and new captives were forced to kill or beat others to bind them to the group. Survey research by the SWAY project estimated that some 60,000–80,000 young people were abducted over the course of the war.

The LRA punished civilians it accused of supporting the government by cutting off lips, ears and limbs and by massacres. Some 170 or more people were killed at Atiak in April 1995; in October 1996, 139 girls were abducted from St Mary's College, Aboke, and the deputy headmistress, Sister Rachele Fassera, followed the rebels into the bush and secured the release of 109 of them. At Barlonyo camp in February 2004 more than 120 people, by some local accounts over 300, were killed. Night after night tens of thousands of 'night commuters', mostly children, walked into Gulu, Kitgum and other towns to sleep in church compounds, hospitals and bus stations to avoid abduction.

The government's response also brought great suffering. From 1996 the army ordered rural Acholi into 'protected villages'; by 2005 around 1.8 million people in northern Uganda lived in squalid, poorly defended camps. A 2005 survey by Uganda's Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization estimated roughly 1,000 excess deaths a week in the camps of Acholi, Lango and Teso. Government soldiers were accused of killings, rapes and torture, and earlier, in 1989, dozens of detainees suffocated in a railway wagon at Mukura in Teso. Operation Iron Fist (2002), a Ugandan offensive into Sudan, provoked LRA expansion into Lango and Teso.

Catholic, Anglican and Muslim leaders formed the Acholi Religious Leaders' Peace Initiative (ARLPI) in 1997–98. They lobbied for the Amnesty Act of 2000, met LRA commanders in the bush and promoted Acholi reconciliation rituals such as mato oput. In 2005 the International Criminal Court issued its first arrest warrants against Kony, Vincent Otti, Raska Lukwiya, Okot Odhiambo and Dominic Ongwen; religious and civic leaders debated whether international prosecution helped or hindered peace. Talks mediated by South Sudan in Juba from 2006 brought a cessation of hostilities, and northern Uganda has been largely peaceful since, but Kony never signed the final agreement in 2008.

The LRA, by then based in Garamba National Park in DR Congo, was attacked by Ugandan, Congolese and South Sudanese forces in Operation Lightning Thunder in December 2008; it retaliated with the 'Christmas massacres' in north-eastern Congo, killing several hundred people, and in December 2009 killed over 300 in the Makombo area. Small LRA groups then roamed the Central African Republic and the Kafia Kingi enclave on the Sudan border. The 2012 'Kony 2012' video by the American charity Invisible Children brought global attention but was criticised by Ugandan and academic observers for simplifying the conflict. US special forces advised the African Union mission against the LRA from 2011 until 2017, by which time the group had dwindled to a few hundred people. Ongwen, himself abducted as a child, was convicted by the ICC in 2021 and sentenced to 25 years; Kony remains at large, and in 2025 the ICC held a confirmation-of-charges hearing in his absence.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Alice Lakwena and Joseph Kony presented their movements as spiritual purification of Acholi society and of Uganda. Kony claimed to receive orders from spirits, enforced prohibitions on certain foods, alcohol and sex outside his rules, used holy water and oil in initiation, and repeatedly told interviewers that he wanted Uganda governed by the Ten Commandments. LRA statements and songs mixed Christian prayers and hymns with spirit beliefs, and at times Kony adopted Islamic practices to please his Sudanese patrons. Acholi church leaders rejected these claims as a perversion of Christianity, while the government used the movement's strangeness to portray the war as mere fanaticism rather than a political conflict.
religiousCauses: The Holy Spirit Movement's message of purifying Acholi society from the guilt and violence of the civil wars attracted demoralised soldiers and villagers in 1986–87.
Kony's claim to spirit possession gave him charismatic authority and was used to discipline abductees, who were told the spirits could see their thoughts.
A promise to rule by the Ten Commandments and to cleanse Uganda gave the movement a moral vocabulary drawn from Christian teaching.
Spiritual rituals of initiation and taboo bound abductees to the group and made escape seem spiritually as well as physically dangerous.
otherCauses: The long north–south divide in Ugandan politics and the army, and the Acholi's sudden loss of power and status when Museveni took power in 1986.
Abuses by the National Resistance Army in the north in 1986–88, including killings and the looting of Acholi cattle.
Sudan's support for the LRA from about 1994 in retaliation for Uganda's backing of the Sudan People's Liberation Army.
Weak state presence, poverty and the availability of arms in the borderlands of Uganda, Sudan, Congo and the Central African Republic.
The government's preference for a military solution and its forced encampment policy, which alienated many Acholi.
triggers: The NRA's capture of Kampala in January 1986 and the flight of defeated northern soldiers.
The defeat of Alice Lakwena's Holy Spirit Movement near Jinja in late 1987, leaving Kony's group as the main spirit-led rebellion.
The collapse of the Bigombe peace talks in 1994 and the beginning of Sudanese support.

timeline.text: Yoweri Museveni's National Resistance Army takes Kampala; northern resistance begins.
Alice Lakwena's Holy Spirit Mobile Forces march south and are defeated near Jinja; Joseph Kony forms his own movement.
Peace talks led by Betty Bigombe collapse; Sudan begins arming the LRA.
LRA massacre at Atiak in April.
139 girls abducted from St Mary's College, Aboke; the army begins forcing rural Acholi into camps.
Catholic, Anglican and Muslim leaders form the Acholi Religious Leaders' Peace Initiative.
Uganda passes the Amnesty Act after lobbying by religious and civic leaders.
Massacre at Barlonyo camp near Lira in February.
The ICC issues arrest warrants for Kony and four commanders; around 1.8 million people live in camps.
Juba peace talks begin and a cessation of hostilities brings calm to northern Uganda.
Kony fails to sign the Final Peace Agreement; Operation Lightning Thunder attacks LRA camps in Garamba, followed by the Christmas massacres in Congo.
LRA kills over 300 people around Makombo in north-eastern Congo in December.
Uganda and the United States end their military hunt for Kony as the LRA dwindles.
The ICC convicts Dominic Ongwen of war crimes and crimes against humanity and sentences him to 25 years.

keyPeople.name: Alice Auma (Lakwena)
keyPeople.role: Spirit medium and leader of the Holy Spirit Movement
keyPeople.focus: Claimed possession by the spirit Lakwena and led an army bound by ritual rules on a march to Kampala in 1987.
keyPeople.outcome: Defeated near Jinja in 1987; lived in a refugee camp in Kenya until her death in 2007.

keyPeople.name: Joseph Kony
keyPeople.role: Founder and leader of the Lord's Resistance Army
keyPeople.focus: Claimed spiritual guidance, directed abductions and massacres in Uganda, Sudan, Congo and the Central African Republic.
keyPeople.outcome: Indicted by the ICC in 2005 and still at large; the ICC held a confirmation-of-charges hearing in his absence in 2025.

keyPeople.name: Dominic Ongwen
keyPeople.focus: Abducted as a boy, rose to command and led attacks on camps including Lukodi and Pajule.
keyPeople.outcome: Surrendered in 2015; convicted by the ICC in 2021 on 61 counts and sentenced to 25 years, a case that raised hard questions about victims who become perpetrators.

keyPeople.name: Yoweri Museveni
keyPeople.focus: Pursued mainly military solutions and ordered the forced encampment of the northern population.
keyPeople.outcome: Remained in power; referred the LRA situation to the ICC in 2003.

keyPeople.name: John Baptist Odama
keyPeople.role: Catholic Archbishop of Gulu and chairman of the Acholi Religious Leaders' Peace Initiative
keyPeople.focus: Pressed for dialogue and amnesty, met LRA commanders and in 2003 slept among the night commuters in Gulu to draw attention to their plight.
keyPeople.outcome: Became a leading African voice for negotiated peace and reconciliation.

keyPeople.name: Macleord Baker Ochola II
keyPeople.role: Anglican Bishop of Kitgum and vice-chairman of ARLPI
keyPeople.focus: Despite the death of his wife in a landmine explosion and an attack on his daughter, campaigned for forgiveness, amnesty and traditional reconciliation.
keyPeople.outcome: Remembered as a symbol of costly peacemaking.

keyPeople.name: Rachele Fassera
keyPeople.role: Comboni sister and deputy headmistress of St Mary's College, Aboke
keyPeople.focus: Followed the LRA after the abduction of 139 schoolgirls in October 1996 and negotiated the release of 109 of them.
keyPeople.outcome: Campaigned internationally for the remaining 'Aboke girls', most of whom eventually returned.

keyPeople.name: Betty Bigombe
keyPeople.focus: Led face-to-face talks with Kony in 1993–94 and again in 2004–05.
keyPeople.outcome: Her talks failed but laid groundwork for the Juba process.

casualties.note: No reliable total exists. Violent deaths in northern Uganda are usually given as tens of thousands, but deaths from disease and malnutrition in the government's camps were larger: a 2005 Ministry of Health/WHO survey estimated about 1,000 excess deaths a week in the camps of northern Uganda. The SWAY survey estimated 60,000–80,000 young people abducted, and around 1.8 million people were displaced at the peak. After 2008 the LRA killed more than 2,000 civilians in Congo, the Central African Republic and South Sudan according to Human Rights Watch and the LRA Crisis Tracker.

effects: Almost the entire rural Acholi population was displaced into camps for a decade, destroying farming, education and traditional social structures.
A generation of former abductees, including many 'child mothers', faced trauma and stigma on return, and the debate over amnesty and justice shaped later transitional justice in Uganda.
The ICC's first arrest warrants (2005) and the Ongwen trial made the LRA a test case for international criminal justice and its relationship to peace negotiations.
LRA violence after 2008 displaced hundreds of thousands in north-eastern Congo and the eastern Central African Republic.
Uganda's Amnesty Act of 2000 allowed tens of thousands of combatants and abductees to return, though it was later restricted for senior commanders.
effectsOnChurch: Parishes, mission hospitals and schools such as Lacor Hospital in Gulu became shelters for night commuters and the displaced.
Catechists, priests and sisters were among those killed or abducted, and mission stations were repeatedly attacked.
The Acholi Religious Leaders' Peace Initiative became a model of Christian–Muslim co-operation for peace in Africa.
Churches promoted combined Christian and Acholi rituals of reconciliation, prompting theological debate about forgiveness and justice.
conflicts.legacy: The LRA is often cited as an example of 'Christian terrorism', but historians caution that it was a millenarian spirit movement rooted in Uganda's political conflicts rather than an expression of the churches' faith. Its most lasting religious legacy is the peace work of Acholi church and Muslim leaders, who insisted that the war needed dialogue and reconciliation as well as military and judicial answers.

dissenters.text: Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox and Muslim leaders who from 1997–98 campaigned for amnesty and negotiation and acted as go-betweens with the LRA.

dissenters.name: John Baptist Odama
dissenters.text: Archbishop of Gulu who repeatedly met rebels, criticised abuses by both sides and lived among the night commuters.

dissenters.name: Macleord Baker Ochola II
dissenters.text: Anglican bishop who forgave those responsible for his own family's suffering and argued for restorative justice.

dissenters.name: Rachele Fassera

conflicts.name: Christian–Muslim violence in Nigeria
conflicts.religionRoleNote: Nigeria is divided roughly equally between Muslims, concentrated in the north, and Christians, concentrated in the south and the Middle Belt, and since the 1980s religion has become the main banner under which local, ethnic and political conflicts are fought. Scholars such as Toyin Falola, Adam Higazi and Alexander Thurston and bodies such as the International Crisis Group and Human Rights Watch stress that most episodes also turn on 'indigene' versus 'settler' rights, land and grazing, control of local government, elections, poverty and police impunity, and that the jihadist Boko Haram insurgency has killed more Muslims than Christians. Christian bodies such as the Christian Association of Nigeria (CAN), advocacy groups such as Open Doors and some foreign politicians argue that Christians in the north and Middle Belt face systematic persecution that is downplayed as 'farmer–herder' or 'communal' conflict; the Nigerian government and many Muslim leaders reject this framing. Both perspectives agree that religious identity now shapes how violence is mobilised, remembered and avenged, which makes religion a major factor even where it is not the original cause.

conflicts.summary: Since the Maitatsine riots of 1980, Nigeria has suffered recurrent waves of killing in which Christian and Muslim identity has been the dividing line: riots in Kano, Kafanchan and Kaduna, the Jos crises from 2001, reprisal massacres in Plateau State, and the Boko Haram insurgency in the north-east. Rural violence between farming communities, mostly Christian, and Fulani herders, mostly Muslim, has become the deadliest form of violence in the Middle Belt. Atrocities have been committed by members of both faiths and by the security forces, while Christian and Muslim leaders have also pioneered celebrated interfaith peace work.
conflicts.story:
British colonial rule (1900–60) joined the Muslim emirates of the north, where Christian missions were largely excluded under indirect rule, with a largely Christianised south and a religiously mixed 'Middle Belt'. After independence, the civil war of 1967–70 was fought mainly over ethnicity and oil but was presented by Biafran propaganda partly as a defence of Christians. From the late 1970s debates over a federal Sharia court of appeal, Nigeria's admission to the Organisation of the Islamic Conference in 1986 and the competition between Christian and Muslim revival movements politicised religion at the national level.

The first great outbreak, the Maitatsine uprising in Kano in December 1980, pitted a heterodox Muslim sect against the police and army and left 4,177 dead according to the official tribunal; it was not a Christian–Muslim conflict, but it set a pattern of urban religious riots. In March 1987 a dispute at the College of Education, Kafanchan, sparked clashes between Christian and Muslim students that spread to Kaduna, Zaria and Katsina, with churches and mosques burned. In 1992 land and market disputes between Atyap and Hausa in Zangon Kataf led to hundreds of deaths and reprisals in Kaduna. When Zamfara and eleven other northern states extended Sharia to criminal law in 1999–2001, Christian protests in Kaduna in February and May 2000 led to fighting in which around 2,000 or more people, Christians and Muslims, were killed.

Jos, the capital of Plateau State, became the epicentre in the 2000s. The appointment of a Hausa Muslim to a local post triggered riots in September 2001 in which about 1,000 people died. In February 2004 Muslim attackers killed dozens of Christians in a church at Yelwa; in May Tarok Christian militias retaliated by killing some 700 Muslims there, and in Kano Muslim crowds then killed more than 200 Christians. Disputed local elections in Jos in November 2008 led to some 700 deaths, including more than 130 people killed by security forces. In January 2010 Christian youths killed about 150 Muslims at Kuru Karama, and in March 2010 Fulani attackers killed more than 200 Berom Christians at Dogo Nahawa. After the April 2011 presidential election, riots and reprisals across the north killed more than 800 people in three days.

Boko Haram, founded around 2002 by the preacher Mohammed Yusuf in Maiduguri, rejected Western education and the secular state. After its 2009 uprising was crushed and Yusuf was killed in police custody, it returned under Abubakar Shekau as a terrorist insurgency: it bombed the UN building in Abuja (2011), St Theresa's Catholic Church at Madalla on Christmas Day 2011 and many other churches, mosques, markets and schools, and abducted 276 schoolgirls, most of them Christian, from Chibok in April 2014. By 2014 it controlled territory around Gwoza; a split in 2016 produced the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP). Military operations, a regional task force and vigilante groups pushed the insurgents back, but security forces were accused by Amnesty International of mass extrajudicial killings and deaths in detention. The insurgency has also killed very large numbers of Muslims, including at Baga in 2015.

Since the mid-2010s the deadliest violence in the Middle Belt has been between farming communities, predominantly Christian, and Fulani herders, predominantly Muslim, driven by land pressure, desertification, cattle theft, the collapse of grazing routes, banditry and impunity. Attacks on villages in Plateau, Benue and southern Kaduna, such as the killings around Barkin Ladi in June 2018, the Christmas Eve attacks in Bokkos and Barkin Ladi in 2023 and the massacre at Yelwata in Benue in June 2025, killed hundreds of Christians, while reprisal killings of Fulani and Muslim travellers, such as on the Rukuba road near Jos in August 2021, also occurred. Gunmen killed about 40 worshippers at St Francis Xavier Church, Owo, on Pentecost Sunday 2022, and in May 2022 the Christian student Deborah Samuel Yakubu was lynched in Sokoto over an alleged blasphemy.

The question of how to name the violence has become an international issue. The United States designated Nigeria a 'Country of Particular Concern' for religious freedom in 2020, removed the designation in 2021 and restored it in 2025; Nigerian officials and many analysts objected that this misrepresented a complex security crisis affecting Muslims as well as Christians, while Christian groups welcomed it. Throughout, interfaith bodies such as the Nigeria Inter-Religious Council and the Interfaith Mediation Centre in Kaduna have worked to contain violence.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Rioters on both sides have attacked churches and mosques and used religious slogans; Muslim crowds have shouted 'Allahu akbar' and Christian militias have invoked defence of the faith. Boko Haram's leaders openly declared jihad against Christians, the Nigerian state and Muslims they considered apostates, and Shekau boasted of abducting Christian girls. Some Christian leaders have described the killings of Christians as a genocide or a jihad by Fulani herders, while Muslim leaders have pointed to massacres of Muslims by Christian militias. Disputes over Sharia, blasphemy and the place of religion in the federal constitution have kept religious identity at the centre of politics.
religiousCauses: The extension of Sharia criminal law in twelve northern states in 1999–2001 alarmed Christian minorities and triggered the Kaduna riots of 2000.
Competition between expanding Pentecostal and evangelical churches and Islamic reform movements such as Izala sharpened religious boundaries from the 1980s.
Boko Haram's Salafi-jihadist ideology explicitly targets Christians, churches and Muslims who participate in the secular state.
Blasphemy accusations, as in the Kaduna 'Miss World' riots of 2002 and the killing of Deborah Samuel Yakubu in 2022, have repeatedly triggered mob violence.
Memories of previous massacres are framed in religious terms, so that revenge attacks target whole faith communities.
otherCauses: The 'indigene' versus 'settler' system, which ties access to land, jobs and political office to ethnic origin, as in the Hausa–Berom contest over Jos.
Competition for farmland and grazing, aggravated by population growth, desertification and the breakdown of traditional grazing routes.
Elections and patronage politics in which politicians mobilise religious and ethnic blocs.
Poverty, youth unemployment and the weakness of education in the north-east, which fed recruitment into Boko Haram.
Impunity: very few perpetrators of mass killings have been prosecuted, and security forces have themselves committed abuses.
Banditry, kidnapping for ransom and the circulation of small arms across the Sahel.
triggers: Disputes over appointments and local elections in Jos in 2001 and 2008.
The adoption of Sharia criminal codes in Zamfara and other northern states from 1999.
The killing of Mohammed Yusuf in police custody in July 2009, which turned Boko Haram into an insurgency.
Cattle rustling and killings of herders or farmers that set off cycles of reprisal attacks in rural Plateau, Benue and Kaduna.

casualties.note: No single estimate covers these overlapping conflicts. Human Rights Watch documented thousands of deaths in inter-communal violence in Plateau and Kaduna States alone between 2001 and 2013. For the Boko Haram/ISWAP insurgency, a 2021 UNDP study estimated nearly 350,000 deaths in north-east Nigeria by the end of 2020, about 35,000 of them direct conflict deaths and the rest from hunger and disease; the majority of the insurgency's victims were Muslims. Farmer–herder and bandit violence has killed thousands more each year since the mid-2010s, with figures from the Council on Foreign Relations' Nigeria Security Tracker, ACLED and church or Muslim groups differing widely depending on how deaths are classified.

effects: Jos, Kaduna and other cities became segregated into Christian and Muslim neighbourhoods.
Over two million people were displaced in the north-east by the Boko Haram insurgency, with major humanitarian crises around Lake Chad.
Religious identity became a central factor in elections and in debates over the presidency's 'zoning' between north and south.
Security forces' abuses and failures to prosecute perpetrators deepened distrust of the state and encouraged self-defence militias.
International advocacy has turned the killings into a foreign-policy issue, especially in the United States.
effectsOnChurch: Hundreds of churches were destroyed and many congregations in the north-east and Middle Belt were scattered or displaced.
Clergy and seminarians have been killed or kidnapped for ransom, making Nigeria one of the most dangerous countries for priests and pastors.
The Christian Association of Nigeria became a powerful political voice, and Christian identity politics grew in the north.
Church-led peace and dialogue initiatives, often with Muslim partners, became an important part of Nigerian Christianity.
Northern Christians have migrated south or into enclaves, changing the religious map of northern cities.
conflicts.legacy: Nigeria, home to Africa's largest Christian and Muslim populations, is often seen as a test of whether the two faiths can share a modern state. Its history shows both cycles of religiously framed revenge, with victims on each side, and some of the world's most influential grassroots interfaith peacemaking.

conflicts.name: Séléka and anti-balaka in the Central African Republic
conflicts.religionRoleNote: The Central African Republic had little history of religious conflict before 2012; the war began as a rebellion by marginalised northern armed groups seeking power and resources. Because the Séléka coalition was overwhelmingly Muslim, including fighters from Chad and Sudan, and because its abuses fell mainly on non-Muslims, the anti-balaka militias that rose against it took revenge on Muslim civilians in general, and the conflict came to be fought along Christian–Muslim lines. Researchers such as Louisa Lombard and Roland Marchal, the International Crisis Group and the UN Commission of Inquiry (2014) stress that religion was a marker of identity, belonging and supposed foreignness rather than a theological cause; anti-balaka fighters relied heavily on protective amulets (gris-gris) rather than Christian doctrine, and Catholic, Protestant and Muslim leaders jointly denied that it was a religious war. Others note that Islamist rhetoric among some Séléka commanders and the targeting of churches and mosques gave the violence a genuinely religious dimension in the eyes of victims.

conflicts.summary: In March 2013 the Séléka, a coalition of mostly Muslim rebels from the north-east, overthrew President François Bozizé and unleashed a wave of looting and killing. Mostly Christian and animist anti-balaka militias rose against them and, from December 2013, carried out reprisal massacres and expulsions of Muslim civilians that a UN inquiry described as ethnic cleansing. The country's Catholic archbishop, the head of its Islamic council and the president of its Evangelical Alliance became internationally known for travelling together to insist that this was not a war of religion.
conflicts.story:
The former French colony of Oubangui-Chari became independent in 1960 under the shadow of its founding father Barthélemy Boganda, a Catholic priest, who died in an air crash in 1959. Coups, the rule of Jean-Bédel Bokassa (1966–79) and chronic misrule left the state weak beyond Bangui. Muslims, perhaps 10–15 per cent of the population, were concentrated in the neglected north-east and in trade, and were often regarded by other Central Africans as foreigners from Chad or Sudan. François Bozizé took power in a coup in 2003; a series of northern rebellions followed, and peace agreements in 2007–08 were poorly implemented.

In December 2012 several northern rebel groups formed the Séléka ('alliance' in Sango) and swept south from Ndélé and Bria. A ceasefire signed in Libreville in January 2013 broke down, and on 24 March 2013 Séléka fighters captured Bangui. Their leader Michel Djotodia became the country's first Muslim head of state. Séléka units, swollen by Chadian and Sudanese fighters, looted, raped and killed across the west and centre, burning villages around Bossangoa and attacking churches and clergy; many Central Africans saw Muslim neighbours as collaborators. Djotodia formally dissolved the Séléka in September 2013 but could not control it.

In response, local self-defence groups known as anti-balaka (roughly 'anti-machete' or 'invulnerable to bullets'), joined by soldiers loyal to Bozizé, attacked Séléka positions and Muslim communities. On 5 December 2013 they attacked Bangui; in the following days around 1,000 people were killed in the capital, and Séléka fighters killed Christians in reprisal. The same day the UN Security Council authorised the French Operation Sangaris and the African-led MISCA force. Djotodia resigned in January 2014 and Catherine Samba-Panza became interim president, but anti-balaka violence against Muslims intensified. Mosques were destroyed, Muslims were lynched, and tens of thousands fled to Chad and Cameroon or were trapped in enclaves such as PK5 in Bangui, Boda and Carnot. Amnesty International described 'ethnic cleansing' in the west, and the UN Commission of Inquiry in December 2014 concluded that anti-balaka forces had carried out ethnic cleansing of Muslims and that both sides had committed crimes against humanity, though it did not find genocidal intent.

In these months churches, mosques and mission stations became refuges. Archbishop Dieudonné Nzapalainga of Bangui sheltered Imam Omar Kobine Layama in his residence, and with Pastor Nicolas Guérékoyamé-Gbangou they formed the Interfaith Platform, touring the country and appealing abroad for peacekeepers. At Bossemptélé the Catholic priest Bernard Kinvi protected Muslims in his mission hospital, and at Carnot and elsewhere Catholic parishes housed hundreds of Muslims under anti-balaka threat. Pope Francis visited Bangui in November 2015, opening the Jubilee of Mercy there and visiting the Koudoukou mosque in PK5, a visit followed by elections that brought Faustin-Archange Touadéra to power in 2016.

The war did not end. The UN mission MINUSCA took over in September 2014, but ex-Séléka factions such as the FPRC and Ali Darassa's mainly Fulani UPC controlled much of the north and east, while anti-balaka groups fought them and each other. In 2017 UPC fighters attacked Muslims sheltering in the Catholic minor seminary at Bangassou after anti-balaka attacks there, and Bishop Juan José Aguirre refused to abandon them. The Khartoum peace agreement of February 2019 brought armed groups into government but did not hold. Russian Wagner Group contractors arrived from 2018 and, with Rwandan troops, helped the government repel a 2020–21 rebel offensive; UN experts and Human Rights Watch later documented killings of civilians, including Muslim Fulani, by Wagner and national forces.

Accountability has been partial. A hybrid Special Criminal Court began work in Bangui in 2018, and in July 2025 the International Criminal Court convicted the anti-balaka leaders Alfred Yekatom and Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona of war crimes and crimes against humanity; the ICC also tried the former Séléka official Mahamat Said Abdel Kani. Most Muslims expelled from the west in 2014 had not returned years later, and large parts of the country remained outside state control.
conflicts.nameOfGod: The anti-balaka were widely called 'Christian militias' in international media, and some fighters wore crosses and spoke of defending Christians, but most relied on traditional amulets believed to make them invulnerable, and the Catholic and Protestant churches publicly disowned them. Some Séléka commanders used Islamic language, attacked churches and treated non-Muslims as enemies, while ordinary Muslims were labelled 'Chadians' and foreigners. Religious leaders of both faiths repeatedly declared that the conflict was political and criminal, not a holy war, and churches and mosques alike served as sanctuaries.
religiousCauses: Séléka abuses fell disproportionately on Christian and animist communities, and attacks on churches and clergy encouraged a reading of the war as Muslim aggression.
Religious identity was conflated with nationality, so that Muslims were treated as foreigners and collaborators of Chadian and Sudanese fighters.
Some commanders on both sides used religious rhetoric to mobilise fighters and justify attacks on mosques or churches.
Rumour, sermons and media in a highly polarised atmosphere spread fear that each faith community intended to destroy the other.
otherCauses: Decades of state failure, coups and neglect of the north-east, which had almost no roads, schools or administration.
Competition for diamonds, gold, cattle and trade routes, and long-standing tensions between farmers and Fulani pastoralists.
Regional interference, especially by Chad and Sudan, and the free movement of armed men and weapons across porous borders.
Bozizé's failure to implement peace agreements and to integrate former rebels.
The collapse of the national army after the Séléka seizure of power, which left communities to defend themselves.
triggers: The Séléka offensive of December 2012 and capture of Bangui on 24 March 2013.
Séléka massacres and village burnings around Bossangoa in mid-2013.
The anti-balaka attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013 and the reprisal killings that followed.

casualties.note: No reliable total exists. Thousands of civilians were killed in 2013–14 alone (around 1,000 in Bangui in early December 2013), and killings continued in later years in the centre and east; tallies by the UN, ACLED and humanitarian agencies are incomplete because of lack of access. At the peak in 2014 roughly a fifth of the population, over one million people, were internally displaced or refugees, and most of the Muslim population of the west was driven out.

effects: The country's Muslim population was largely expelled from the west and south-west, creating enclaves and refugee populations in Chad and Cameroon.
The state lost control of most of its territory to shifting armed groups, many of which became predatory economic enterprises.
A large UN peacekeeping mission (MINUSCA) and, later, Russian private military contractors became central to the country's security.
The Special Criminal Court and ICC cases created the first judicial accountability for atrocities in the conflict.
Chronic humanitarian crisis, with a large share of the population dependent on aid.
effectsOnChurch: Catholic and Protestant missions became shelters for tens of thousands of displaced people, both Christian and Muslim.
Several priests and religious were killed and many churches and mosques were looted or destroyed.
The Interfaith Platform of Nzapalainga, Layama and Guérékoyamé-Gbangou became a model of joint religious peacebuilding.
Pope Francis's 2015 visit, a rare papal visit to an active war zone, gave the local church international attention.
Churches faced the difficulty of disciplining members and catechists involved in anti-balaka violence.
conflicts.legacy: The Central African conflict is a case study in how a political rebellion became a sectarian war once religion was equated with belonging. It is remembered both for the expulsion of Muslims by militias drawn from Christian communities and for the Christian and Muslim leaders who risked their lives to protect members of the other faith.

conflicts.name: Russia's war on Ukraine and the "Russian world" doctrine
conflicts.religionRoleNote: Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 and full-scale invasion in 2022 were driven above all by geopolitics, imperial nationalism and the Kremlin's refusal to accept a sovereign, Western-leaning Ukraine; Vladimir Putin's own justifications centred on NATO, security and the claim that Russians and Ukrainians are 'one people'. Religion enters through the 'Russian world' (russkii mir) ideology, which presents Russia, Ukraine and Belarus as a single civilisation born at the baptism of Kyiv in 988, and through Patriarch Kirill of Moscow's open blessing of the war as a metaphysical struggle against Western decadence. Scholars such as Serhii Plokhy treat religion as one strand of a broader nationalist ideology; Orthodox theologians who signed the 2022 Volos Academy declaration condemned the 'Russian world' teaching as a heresy that had helped prepare the war; others (e.g. Marlene Laruelle) stress that the concept is fluid and largely instrumental, used by the state for soft power. The war has also deepened a church conflict between Moscow and Kyiv over Ukrainian Orthodox independence, so religion is both a legitimising ideology and a field of the conflict, but not its primary cause.

sides.name: Russian Federation and, in 2014–22, the Russian-backed 'Donetsk' and 'Luhansk People's Republics'
sides.faith: Majority Russian Orthodox (Moscow Patriarchate) by heritage, with Muslims and others; the war is supported by the Moscow Patriarchate's leadership

sides.name: Ukraine
sides.faith: Religiously plural: Orthodox Church of Ukraine, Ukrainian Orthodox Church, Ukrainian Greek Catholics, Roman Catholics, Protestants, Jews and Muslims

conflicts.summary: Russia seized Crimea and fomented war in eastern Ukraine in 2014, then launched a full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022, the largest war in Europe since 1945. The Kremlin's case drew on the 'Russian world' idea of a single Orthodox East Slavic civilisation, and Patriarch Kirill of Moscow framed the war as a holy struggle against Western moral decay, while Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant leaders around the world, and many Orthodox Christians in Ukraine and Russia, condemned it. The war has killed many tens of thousands, devastated Ukrainian cities and deepened the split within world Orthodoxy.
conflicts.story:
Both Russia and Ukraine trace their Christianity to the baptism of Prince Volodymyr (Vladimir) of Kyiv in 988. After the Mongol conquest the centre of Rus' Orthodoxy shifted to Moscow; the Metropolis of Kyiv was transferred from the jurisdiction of Constantinople to that of Moscow in 1686, a transfer Constantinople later declared to have been temporary. Under the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union, Ukrainian identity and Ukrainian-language church life were suppressed, and in 1946 the Soviet state forcibly merged the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church into the Russian Orthodox Church. After Ukrainian independence in 1991 Orthodoxy split between the Ukrainian Orthodox Church under Moscow, the Kyiv Patriarchate led from 1995 by Filaret Denysenko, and the small Autocephalous Orthodox Church, while the Greek Catholics re-emerged from the underground.

From the 2000s Russian officials and church leaders promoted the idea of a 'Russian world' (russkii mir): a transnational civilisation of Russian language, culture and Orthodox faith centred on Moscow and including Ukraine and Belarus. Putin created the Russkiy Mir Foundation in 2007, and Patriarch Kirill, elected in 2009, made the concept central to his speeches, describing Kyiv as the 'Jerusalem' of Holy Rus'. When the Euromaidan protests of 2013–14 toppled President Viktor Yanukovych, Ukrainian Greek Catholic and Kyiv Patriarchate clergy prayed on the Maidan and St Michael's Golden-Domed Monastery sheltered protesters. Russia then annexed Crimea in March 2014 and backed armed separatists in Donetsk and Luhansk; in eight years of war in the Donbas over 14,000 people were killed, around 3,400 of them civilians, including the 298 people aboard flight MH17. In occupied areas, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Kyiv Patriarchate, Protestant and Jehovah's Witness communities faced harassment and seizures.

The church conflict escalated in parallel. In 2018 the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople moved to grant independence (autocephaly) to a united Ukrainian church; Moscow broke communion with Constantinople in October 2018, and in January 2019 Patriarch Bartholomew handed the tomos of autocephaly to Metropolitan Epiphanius of the new Orthodox Church of Ukraine. In July 2021 Putin published an essay, 'On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians', which invoked the 'common baptismal font' of 988 and denied that Ukraine had a separate national history.

On 24 February 2022 Russia invaded from the north, east and south. Its attempt to take Kyiv failed and its forces withdrew from the north in late March, leaving behind evidence of mass killings of civilians at Bucha and elsewhere. The siege of Mariupol devastated the city; the drama theatre where hundreds of civilians sheltered was bombed on 16 March. Ukrainian counter-offensives retook Kharkiv province and Kherson in autumn 2022, but the front then largely stabilised in the east and south, with grinding battles at Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Pokrovsk. Russia's missile and drone campaign against cities and power infrastructure has killed thousands of civilians; Russia annexed four Ukrainian provinces in September 2022, and the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023 over the deportation of Ukrainian children. UN monitors also documented abuses by Ukrainian forces, including the ill-treatment and some summary executions of Russian prisoners of war, and civilian deaths from Ukrainian shelling in Russian-held areas, on a much smaller scale.

Patriarch Kirill gave the invasion his public support. In a sermon on 6 March 2022 he described the conflict in Donbas as a 'metaphysical' struggle over whether people would accept Western values such as gay pride parades; in September 2022 he told soldiers that sacrifice in the performance of military duty 'washes away all sins'; and in March 2024 the World Russian People's Council, which he chairs, described the war as a 'holy war' defending Holy Rus' and the world against globalism and 'satanism'. By contrast Metropolitan Onufriy of the Moscow-linked Ukrainian Orthodox Church condemned the invasion on its first day as a repetition of 'the sin of Cain', and in May 2022 his church's council declared its 'full independence' from Moscow while stopping short of autocephaly. Ukraine's government, suspecting some UOC clergy of collaboration, searched its monasteries, prosecuted dozens of clergy and in August 2024 passed a law allowing the banning of religious organisations linked to the Russian Orthodox Church; UN human rights monitors and some religious freedom advocates voiced concern, while Ukrainian authorities called it a matter of national security. In occupied territories Russian authorities closed or seized Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Orthodox Church of Ukraine and Protestant congregations and detained clergy, some of whom were tortured or killed.

The war's human cost has been immense. UN monitors had verified more than 13,000 civilian deaths by mid-2025 and say the true figure is considerably higher; military deaths on both sides number in the hundreds of thousands according to Western estimates. Millions of Ukrainians became refugees or internally displaced, and hundreds of churches, mosques and synagogues were damaged or destroyed. Diplomacy in 2025, including direct Russian–Ukrainian talks in Istanbul and US-brokered efforts, produced large prisoner exchanges but no settlement, and Pope Leo XIV, like Pope Francis before him, repeatedly offered the Holy See's mediation.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Russian state and church rhetoric presented the war as the defence of Holy Rus' and traditional Christian values against a decadent, 'satanic' West. Putin invoked the baptism of Kyiv in 988 and in his annexation speech of September 2022 denounced Western 'satanism'; Patriarch Kirill preached that the Donbas conflict was a metaphysical struggle, promised that soldiers who died in their duty would have their sins washed away, and introduced a prayer for the victory of 'Holy Rus'' that clergy were required to read. The Main Cathedral of the Russian Armed Forces at Kubinka, consecrated in 2020, embodied the fusion of military and Orthodox symbolism. On the Ukrainian side clergy of most churches serve as chaplains and the war is widely described as a just war of national defence; the government's measures against the Moscow-linked church were justified as security rather than doctrine.
religiousCauses: The 'Russian world' ideology, embraced by Patriarch Kirill, treats Ukraine as part of a single Orthodox civilisation centred on Moscow and denies its distinct religious and national identity.
The creation of the autocephalous Orthodox Church of Ukraine in 2018–19 was seen in Moscow as a geopolitical defeat and a loss of millions of faithful and historic sites such as Kyiv.
A 'traditional values' discourse shared by the Kremlin and the Moscow Patriarchate framed the West, and a Westward-turning Ukraine, as a moral and spiritual threat.
The close alliance between the Russian state and the Moscow Patriarchate gave the war religious legitimacy and silenced dissenting clergy within Russia.
otherCauses: Putin's imperial nationalism and his view that the collapse of the Soviet Union was a catastrophe and that Ukraine is not a real nation.
Opposition to NATO enlargement and to Ukraine's movement towards the European Union after 2014.
Fear in the Kremlin that a democratic Ukraine could inspire political change in Russia.
Control of Crimea, the Black Sea Fleet at Sevastopol, the industrial Donbas and land access to Crimea.
Miscalculation of Ukrainian resistance and Western unity based on flawed intelligence.
triggers: The Euromaidan revolution and the flight of President Yanukovych in February 2014, followed by the seizure of Crimea.
The failure of the Minsk agreements of 2014–15 to settle the Donbas war.
Russia's military build-up in 2021 and the rejection of its demands for guarantees against NATO enlargement, culminating in recognition of the separatist 'republics' on 21 February 2022.

casualties.note: No reliable overall figure exists while the war continues. For 2014–21 the UN human rights office (OHCHR) counted about 14,000 conflict-related deaths, about 3,400 of them civilians. Since February 2022 the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission had verified more than 13,000 civilian deaths by mid-2025, stating that the real number is higher, especially in occupied Mariupol. Military deaths are state secrets; the independent outlet Mediazona and BBC Russian had confirmed by name more than 100,000 Russian soldiers killed by mid-2025, and Western government and think-tank estimates (e.g. CSIS, 2025) put Russian military deaths at several hundred thousand and Ukrainian military deaths at tens of thousands to around 100,000. These figures are contested and should be treated as rough.

effects: Millions of Ukrainians fled abroad or were internally displaced, and large areas of eastern and southern Ukraine were devastated or occupied.
Russia became subject to extensive Western sanctions and deepened its alignment with China, Iran and North Korea.
Finland and Sweden joined NATO, and European states greatly increased defence spending.
The International Criminal Court and national courts opened investigations into war crimes, including the deportation of Ukrainian children.
Ukrainian national identity, including use of the Ukrainian language and church independence, was greatly strengthened.
effectsOnChurch: Hundreds of churches and other religious sites were damaged or destroyed, according to Ukrainian and international monitors.
Large numbers of parishes moved from the Moscow-linked Ukrainian Orthodox Church to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine, and the UOC distanced itself from Moscow.
The schism between Moscow and Constantinople deepened, and Orthodox churches worldwide were forced to take positions on Kirill's support for the war.
The 'Russian world' teaching was condemned by many Orthodox theologians as ethno-phyletism, a heresy condemned by Constantinople in 1872.
Russian clergy who opposed the war were fined, suspended or defrocked, while some emigrated or joined other jurisdictions.
conflicts.legacy: The war is the clearest twenty-first-century case of a Christian church leadership blessing a war of aggression against a largely Christian neighbour, and it has provoked intense debate within Orthodoxy about nationalism, church–state 'symphony' and the theology of the nation. It has also brought renewed reflection on just war and on the duties of churches, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, to resist the sacralising of violence.

conflicts.name: Christian justifications of slavery and colonial wars
conflicts.region: Atlantic world: Iberia, West and West-Central Africa, the Caribbean and the Americas
conflicts.religionRoleNote: The Atlantic slave trade and the wars of colonial expansion were driven chiefly by profit, labour demand, state power and rivalry between European empires. Christianity contributed in two ways. First, papal bulls such as Dum diversas (1452) and Romanus pontifex (1455) extended the language of crusade against 'Saracens and pagans' to Africa, and theologians, preachers and planters used the conversion of Africans, the 'curse of Ham' and biblical passages regulating slavery to present enslavement and conquest as lawful and even benevolent. Second, churches and religious orders themselves owned plantations and enslaved people. Historians such as David Brion Davis argue that Christianity long accommodated slavery as part of the natural order, while also supplying the moral resources (Quaker conscience, evangelical revival, Catholic natural law, Black Christian prophecy) that eventually fuelled abolition; Willie James Jennings and others stress the role of Christian theology in forming modern ideas of race. Because religion legitimised rather than originated the trade, and Christians stood on both sides of the struggle, its role is best described as contributing.

sides.name: Christian abolitionists and critics of conquest

conflicts.summary: From the Portuguese voyages of the fifteenth century to the abolition of slavery in Brazil in 1888, Christian authorities and thinkers repeatedly gave religious sanction to the enslavement of Africans and to wars against non-Christian peoples. Papal bulls authorised the 'perpetual servitude' of Africans, preachers taught that slavery brought heathens to salvation, and churches, religious orders and missionary societies owned enslaved people. Yet Christians were also among slavery's first and fiercest critics, and the movement that ended the Atlantic trade was led in large part by Quakers, evangelicals and enslaved Christians themselves.
conflicts.story:
Slavery was accepted across the ancient and medieval Mediterranean, and Christian theology since Augustine had treated it as a consequence of sin rather than a natural right; medieval canonists allowed the enslavement of non-Christians captured in a just war. When Portuguese caravels reached West Africa, the chronicler Gomes Eanes de Zurara described the first large sale of Africans at Lagos in 1444 with pity but justified it by the captives' conversion. Pope Nicholas V's bull Dum diversas (1452) authorised King Afonso V to 'invade, search out, capture, vanquish and subdue all Saracens and pagans' and to reduce them to perpetual servitude, and Romanus pontifex (1455) confirmed Portugal's monopoly of the African coast. Alexander VI's Inter caetera (1493) divided newly found lands between Portugal and Spain on condition of evangelisation, the root of what was later called the 'doctrine of discovery'.

In the Spanish Americas the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos denounced the abuse of the Taíno in 1511, and the Requerimiento of 1513 required Indigenous peoples to accept the authority of the pope and the king on pain of war and enslavement. Bartolomé de las Casas fought the enslavement of Indigenous Americans, and the debate at Valladolid in 1550–51 pitted him against Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, who invoked Aristotle's natural slavery. Las Casas had once proposed African labour as an alternative and later repented of it, but the Spanish and Portuguese crowns turned increasingly to enslaved Africans. In Kongo, whose Christian king Afonso I complained to Portugal in 1526 that traders were seizing his free subjects, and in Portuguese Angola, conquered in a series of wars from 1575, captives were commonly baptised en masse at Luanda before embarkation. Jesuits and other orders in Brazil and Spanish America owned plantations worked by enslaved people.

Protestant powers entered the trade in the seventeenth century and developed their own justifications. The 'curse of Ham' (Genesis 9) was widely read as condemning Africans to servitude; preachers cited the Old Testament laws on slavery and the apostolic instruction to slaves to obey their masters. Colonial wars against Native Americans were also framed providentially: after the destruction of the Pequot fort at Mystic in 1637, in which several hundred men, women and children died, the colonial commander John Mason presented the slaughter as God's own judgment on the 'heathen', and during King Philip's War (1675–76) Christian Indian converts were interned on Deer Island in Boston Harbour, where many died. France's Code Noir of 1685 required that enslaved people be baptised Catholic while codifying their status as property. The Society for the Propagation of the Gospel, an Anglican mission society, inherited the Codrington plantations in Barbados in 1710 and worked them with enslaved people, branded with the word 'SOCIETY', until emancipation in 1834–38. George Whitefield campaigned to legalise slavery in Georgia and Jonathan Edwards owned enslaved people.

Christian opposition grew alongside. Capuchin missionaries Francisco José de Jaca and Epifanio de Moirans were imprisoned in Havana in 1681 for refusing absolution to slaveholders; the Afro-Brazilian Lourenço da Silva de Mendouça petitioned Rome against perpetual enslavement in 1684; and German and Dutch Quakers issued the Germantown protest in 1688. Quaker reformers such as Benjamin Lay, John Woolman and Anthony Benezet persuaded the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting to bar slave trading (1758) and slaveholding (1776). John Wesley's Thoughts upon Slavery (1774), the testimony of Olaudah Equiano and the evangelical Clapham circle around William Wilberforce helped secure the British abolition of the slave trade in 1807. Black Christians made the strongest case: Richard Allen founded the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and the Jamaican Baptist deacon Samuel Sharpe led the 1831–32 rising that hastened British emancipation in 1833–34. Pope Gregory XVI condemned the slave trade in 1839.

In the United States, the conflict split the churches. Southern theologians such as Thornton Stringfellow and James Henley Thornwell defended slavery as biblical and divinely ordained, while Frederick Douglass contrasted 'the Christianity of Christ' with 'the slaveholding religion of this land'. The Methodists divided in 1844, the Southern Baptist Convention was formed in 1845 over the right of slaveholders to serve as missionaries, and the Presbyterians split in 1861; each side in the Civil War claimed God's favour. Nat Turner's 1831 revolt in Virginia was inspired by visions and biblical prophecy, and was crushed with bloody reprisals. Slavery ended with the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865, in Cuba in 1886 and in Brazil, the largest importer of enslaved Africans, in 1888.

As the Atlantic trade closed, the rhetoric of Christian civilisation was turned to colonial expansion in Africa. The General Act of the Berlin Conference (1884–85) pledged the powers to protect missionaries and suppress slavery while partitioning the continent, and Cardinal Charles Lavigerie launched an anti-slavery crusade in 1888 aimed at the East African and Saharan trade. King Leopold II's Congo Free State used humanitarian and Christian language while imposing forced labour that killed very large numbers of people; Protestant missionaries such as William Sheppard and Alice Seeley Harris later helped expose its atrocities. In recent decades churches have begun to acknowledge this history: the Southern Baptist Convention apologised in 1995, Georgetown University and the Jesuits acknowledged their sale of 272 enslaved people in 1838, the Church of England's Church Commissioners published research on their ties to the slave trade in 2023, and the Vatican formally repudiated the 'doctrine of discovery' in 2023.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Papal bulls cast the subjugation of Africans as part of the crusade against Islam and paganism and as a means of saving souls. Portuguese and Spanish captives were baptised before shipment; the Requerimiento invoked God, the pope and the Spanish crown before war could be declared. Protestant planters and preachers cited the curse of Ham, Abraham's servants, the Mosaic slave laws and the Pauline command 'Slaves, obey your masters', and taught enslaved people a catechism of obedience. New England Puritans read victories over Native Americans as divine judgment on the 'heathen'. On the other side, abolitionists invoked the unity of humankind in Adam, the Golden Rule and the Exodus, and enslaved Christians sang of deliverance.
religiousCauses: Papal bulls of 1452–1493 granted Christian monarchs the right to conquer non-Christians and to reduce them to perpetual servitude, framing expansion as a continuation of the crusades.
The argument that enslavement brought Africans to baptism and salvation was used from Zurara in the 1440s to American planters in the 1850s.
Readings of the 'curse of Ham' and of biblical slave laws were used to present African slavery as divinely sanctioned.
Providential theology in New England and elsewhere treated victories over Indigenous peoples as God's judgment on heathens.
Churches, religious orders and mission societies owned enslaved people and depended on slave-produced wealth, giving them a stake in the system.
otherCauses: The enormous profits of sugar, tobacco, cotton and other plantation crops, and the demand for labour after Indigenous populations collapsed from disease and violence.
Competition among European empires for land, trade monopolies and naval power.
Pre-existing slavery and warfare in West and West-Central Africa, which allowed European traders to buy captives from African states and merchants.
Emerging ideas of race that placed Africans and Indigenous peoples beneath Europeans.
Colonial settlers' hunger for land, which drove repeated wars against Native American and later African peoples.
triggers: Portuguese voyages down the West African coast and the first large sale of Africans at Lagos, Portugal, in 1444.
The bulls Dum diversas (1452), Romanus pontifex (1455) and Inter caetera (1493).
The rise of sugar plantations in São Tomé, Brazil and the Caribbean from the late fifteenth to seventeenth centuries.
