keyPeople.name: Gomes Eanes de Zurara
keyPeople.focus: His Chronicle of Guinea described the 1444 slave sale at Lagos and justified it by the captives' conversion.
keyPeople.outcome: His account shaped the ideology of Portuguese expansion.

keyPeople.name: Nicholas V
keyPeople.focus: Issued Dum diversas (1452) and Romanus pontifex (1455), authorising Portuguese conquest and enslavement of non-Christians in Africa.
keyPeople.outcome: The bulls were later cited as foundations of the 'doctrine of discovery', which the Vatican repudiated in 2023.

keyPeople.name: Afonso I of Kongo (Mvemba a Nzinga)
keyPeople.focus: Built a Catholic kingdom and took part in the slave trade but protested to João III of Portugal in 1526 against traders seizing his free subjects.
keyPeople.outcome: His letters are among the earliest African written protests against the trade.

keyPeople.name: Bartolomé de las Casas
keyPeople.role: Dominican friar and bishop of Chiapas
keyPeople.focus: Campaigned against Indigenous slavery and conquest, debated Sepúlveda at Valladolid and later repented of his early support for African slavery.
keyPeople.outcome: Regarded as a forerunner of human rights thought.

keyPeople.name: George Whitefield
keyPeople.focus: Preached to enslaved people and criticised their cruel treatment, but campaigned for the legalisation of slavery in Georgia and used enslaved labour for his Bethesda orphanage.
keyPeople.outcome: A symbol of evangelicalism's early accommodation with slavery.

keyPeople.name: John Woolman
keyPeople.focus: Travelled among Quaker slaveholders urging them to free their slaves and wrote Some Considerations on the Keeping of Negroes (1754).
keyPeople.outcome: Helped make Quakers the first major Christian body to reject slaveholding.

keyPeople.name: Samuel Sharpe
keyPeople.focus: Organised the 1831–32 'Baptist War' strike and rising, which planters crushed with mass executions and the burning of chapels.
keyPeople.outcome: Hanged in 1832; the rising hastened British emancipation and he is a National Hero of Jamaica.

keyPeople.name: Thornton Stringfellow
keyPeople.focus: Wrote influential biblical defences of slavery, arguing that God had sanctioned it in both Testaments.
keyPeople.outcome: Representative of the pro-slavery theology defeated in the Civil War.

keyPeople.name: William Wilberforce
keyPeople.focus: Led the parliamentary campaign that abolished the British slave trade in 1807.
keyPeople.outcome: Died days after the Slavery Abolition Act passed the Commons in 1833.

keyPeople.name: Frederick Douglass
keyPeople.focus: Exposed the hypocrisy of 'slaveholding religion' while affirming 'the Christianity of Christ'.
keyPeople.outcome: The leading African American voice of the nineteenth century.

casualties.note: No total can be given for the colonial wars, and religious justification was only one factor among many. For the Atlantic slave trade, the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (Eltis and Richardson) estimates about 12.5 million Africans embarked between 1501 and 1866 and about 10.7 million landed, implying some 1.8 million deaths at sea; millions more died in capture, wars and marches in Africa and in the early years of plantation labour, but these deaths cannot be estimated precisely.

effects: The forced migration of about 12.5 million Africans transformed the demography, economy and culture of the Americas and devastated many African societies.
Racial slavery created enduring patterns of racism and inequality in the Americas.
The 'doctrine of discovery' derived from papal bulls was cited in colonial and later national law, including the US Supreme Court's Johnson v. M'Intosh (1823), to dispossess Indigenous peoples.
Abolition movements, often religious in inspiration, became a model for later humanitarian and human rights campaigns.
Colonial partition of Africa from the 1880s was justified partly by the claim to suppress slavery and spread Christian civilisation.
effectsOnChurch: Black Christianity, including independent churches such as the African Methodist Episcopal Church and the Black Baptist conventions, emerged from slavery and the rejection of segregated white churches.
American Methodists, Baptists and Presbyterians divided over slavery in 1844–61, divisions that shaped American Protestantism for a century or more.
Quakers, Methodists and evangelical Anglicans gained moral authority from their role in abolition.
Churches in Britain, the United States and Europe have since issued apologies and begun reparative projects for their ownership of enslaved people.
African and Caribbean Christians have developed theologies of liberation and reconciliation in response to this history.
conflicts.legacy: The Christian justification of slavery and conquest is among the most painful chapters of church history, and it remains central to debates about race, reparations and the relationship between mission and empire. The same history shows Christian faith inspiring resistance and abolition, and today the descendants of enslaved Africans form a large part of global Christianity.

campaigns.title: Portuguese expansion down the African coast
campaigns.text: Sanctioned by papal bulls, Portuguese ships established trading forts from Arguin to Elmina, a sugar colony on São Tomé, an alliance with Christian Kongo and finally the colony of Angola, which became the largest single source of enslaved Africans.

campaigns.title: The triangular trade and the Middle Passage
campaigns.people: British, French, Dutch and Portuguese slave ships
campaigns.text: Ships carried manufactured goods to West Africa, exchanged them for captives who endured the Middle Passage to the Caribbean and North America, and returned with sugar, tobacco and cotton; Liverpool alone dispatched several thousand slaving voyages before 1807.
